verdict.headline: Hormuz oil shock sent rates to cycle highs; the Fed and Oman talks converge next week
verdict.label: S&P 500 closed the week at 7,656.98, down 0.6%, after four straight losing sessions driven by oil's 9.4% weekly surge to a $100.05 Friday settle on Iran-Hormuz hostilities; core CPI printed 0.3% against a 0.2% estimate and Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 47.8, the second-lowest reading since 1952, with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6%; September 16 hike odds finished the week at roughly 85%; the 10Y yield hit 4.96%, its highest close of this rate cycle; BTC $77,209 on Saturday
verdict.rationale_short:
The week was an oil shock that became an inflation story. WTI crude rose from roughly $91 at Monday's open to a $100.05 settle Friday — a 9.4% weekly gain driven by US-Iran military exchanges in the Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic through the world's most-used energy chokepoint fell to a fraction of normal. Friday reversed the momentum: Iranian state media announced Tehran would meet Gulf states in Oman, crude fell 2.4% to a still-$100 settle, and stocks snapped four losing sessions with the S&P 500 gaining 0.86% to 7,656.98. The week still ended the S&P down 0.6% and the Nasdaq down 0.7%.

The energy move hit a second channel on Friday. August core CPI rose 0.3% from July, a tenth above estimates, with the shelter index jumping to 0.3% after two consecutive months at 0.1% — shelter is roughly a third of core and is not an energy line. Ninety minutes after the open, the University of Michigan put preliminary September sentiment at 47.8, the second-lowest reading since 1952, with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6% from 4.0% and the long-run measure ticking to 3.4%. Anchored long-run expectations are the stated reason a central bank can look through an oil shock. That argument reached the committee in blackout, unable to contextualize it. Futures finished the day pricing roughly 85% probability of a September 16 quarter-point increase, from about 66% before the week started and about 35% a month ago.

The ten-year yield closed the week at 4.96%, its highest of this rate cycle, rising on a day crude fell 2.4% and equity volatility dropped 10.79% — the bond market moved on the policy path, not the energy premium. The thirty-year finished at roughly 5.36%, eight basis points below the 2007 peak of 5.44%. The dollar index sat at 99.00, one point from its formal trigger level. None of the seven formal regime indicators breached their thresholds as of Friday's close, but four are within striking distance: the ten-year four basis points from 5.00%, the thirty-year eight from the 2007 peak, the dollar one point from 100.0, and WTI holding $100 by five cents on the week's clearest de-escalation headline.

The week ahead concentrates three catalysts. GCC diplomats are expected to meet their Iranian counterpart in Oman Monday to discuss a temporary Hormuz shipping arrangement. A confirmed framework before Wednesday changes the framing of the hike from emergency oil-shock response to a planned cycle step, removes the energy input from October CPI, and could take crude sharply below $100. No deal by Wednesday means the committee raises into an unresolved supply shock with year-ahead expectations at 4.6%. August retail sales land at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday — consensus roughly 0.2% against 0.5% in July — putting the growth side of the trade-off in the same session as the 2:00 p.m. FOMC decision and updated dot plot. The 25-basis-point move is priced near-certainty; the dot plot is the read, showing whether this hike closes the cycle or opens a sequence. A dot projecting two or more additional increases past September pushes the long end further toward the 2007 threshold on the thirty-year; a dot showing September as the final move, paired with falling crude, compresses it.

The Friday equity-rate divergence was not a mistake in either market. Stocks priced the partial oil reversal and the AI capital spending news from Dell and Oracle. The rate market priced core CPI and the expectations jump. Both readings are internally consistent, and the Russell 2000's 0.4% gain against the Dow's 0.98% shows the rate-sensitive part of equities sided with the bond market. The thirty-year at 5.36% has the 2007 peak eight basis points above it; whether that level is crossed depends on the dot plot projecting one hike or three.

What would change the picture: a Hormuz framework confirmed before Wednesday removes the energy input from October data and weakens the case for sequential hikes. A dot plot showing September as the final hike, paired with a ten-year that holds below 4.90% post-decision, would say the market reads this as a cycle end rather than a pause. A retail sales print at or above 0.5% in the same session says consumption is outrunning the energy shock, which steepens the curve rather than settling it. BTC at $77,209 Saturday is in its eleventh consecutive session below $80,000 and continues to trade with rate-sensitive assets rather than as a haven; $75,000 is $2,209 below and has not been tested.
verdict.lede_short: The S&P 500 lost 0.6% on the week as oil rose 9.4% on Iran-Hormuz hostilities and core CPI ran a tenth hot, pushing the 10Y yield to 4.96% — its highest close of this rate cycle. Friday brought partial relief when Iran-Oman talks were announced: crude fell 2.4% to a $100.05 settle and stocks snapped a four-session losing streak. The week ahead concentrates three catalysts: Iran-Oman Hormuz talks Monday, retail sales Wednesday morning, and the FOMC decision and dot plot Wednesday afternoon.

supporting_data.label: WTI rose 9.4% on the week to a $100.05 Friday settle — the US-Iran Hormuz conflict cut tanker traffic to a fraction of normal, left US retail diesel at a record and distillate stocks at a seasonal low, and set up Monday's GCC-Iran Oman talks as the week's first binary on whether the energy shock continues into October CPI

The ten-year yield closed Friday at 4.96%, its highest of this rate cycle, rising on a day crude fell 2.4% and equity volatility dropped 10.79% — the bond market is pricing the policy path rather than the energy premium, with four basis points to 5.00% on the ten-year and eight to the 2007 peak of 5.44% on the thirty-year

September 16 hike odds moved to roughly 85% by week's end, up from 35% after July's jobs miss and 66% entering the week — the fifty-point move in a month priced a committee that sees the energy shock and the consumer expectations jump in the same forward view, with the dot plot on Wednesday the remaining read on how many hikes the committee projects

Core CPI rose 0.3% in August against a 0.2% estimate, with the shelter index at 0.3% after two months at 0.1% — shelter is roughly a third of core and is not an energy line, so two non-energy components accelerating in the same month makes a supply-shock explanation harder to sustain at Wednesday's meeting

Preliminary September consumer sentiment fell to 47.8 — the second-lowest reading since 1952 — with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6% from 4.0% and the long-run measure at 3.4%; the survey reached the FOMC in blackout four days before the decision, unable to be contextualized by any committee member

Gulf Cooperation Council diplomats are expected to meet Iran's counterpart in Oman Monday on a temporary Strait of Hormuz shipping arrangement — a confirmed framework before Wednesday's FOMC decision would remove the energy input from October CPI data and change the framing of the hike from an emergency oil-shock response to a planned cycle step

watchlist_mentions.note: WTI settled at $100.05 Friday, down 2.4% on the day Iran-Oman talks were announced and still +9.4% on the week — crude held $100 by five cents on the week's clearest de-escalation headline. GCC diplomats meet Iran's counterpart in Oman Monday; a confirmed framework before Wednesday would be the first event since the conflict began that could take WTI sharply below $100 on a settle.

The ten-year yield closed Friday at 4.96%, its highest of this rate cycle, rising on a day crude fell and equity volatility collapsed — the move is pricing the policy path, not the oil premium. Four basis points separate the ten-year from 5.00%. The thirty-year at roughly 5.36% sits eight basis points below the 2007 peak of 5.44%, a level not crossed since before the Global Financial Crisis.

Trading at $77,209 on Saturday (Crypto.com data; 24h range $77,060-$77,513), in its eleventh consecutive session below $80,000 and essentially flat on the day. BTC continues to track rate-sensitive assets — it took no bid from Friday's equity rally and has not served as a haven during the Hormuz crisis. The $75,000 level is $2,209 below and has not been tested in this rate cycle.

Gold December futures settled at $4,408.90 Friday, essentially flat on a day September 16 hike odds moved to roughly 90% — a traditional safe-haven that declined to sell off into near-certain tightening suggests ongoing haven demand beneath the real-rate pressure. Spot gold was around $4,348 on Saturday. The $4,500 trigger remains $91 above Friday's futures close.

trade_setups.asset: Hormuz shipping arrangement — GCC-Iran talks in Oman, due Monday
trade_setups.thesis: Gulf Cooperation Council diplomats are expected to meet Iran's counterpart in Oman to discuss a temporary Hormuz shipping arrangement. The week's highest-volatility catalyst has no fixed time and nothing on the economic calendar alongside it. A confirmed framework before Wednesday changes the framing of the September hike from emergency oil-shock response to planned cycle step, removes the energy input from October CPI data, and could take crude sharply below $100. No deal by Wednesday means the committee raises into an unresolved supply shock with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6% and no way to address them through communication, since blackout runs through September 17.
trade_setups.entry: WTI's Monday settle is the observable: a close below $100 signals a framework is near or confirmed; a close above $102 signals talks stalled or a new incident occurred. Crude has not closed above $102 since the Oman announcement Friday.
trade_setups.invalidation: A new Hormuz incident over the weekend or Monday morning would push crude back toward $104 and put a second consecutive month of energy pass-through into November CPI data.

trade_setups.asset: Federal Reserve dot plot — September 16, 2:00 p.m. ET
trade_setups.thesis: A 25-basis-point hike to 3.75%-4.00% is priced at roughly 85%; the rate move itself is not the read. The updated Summary of Economic Projections — the committee's median projections for rates, growth, and inflation — is. A dot plot showing two or more additional hikes past September pushes the long end further, with the ten-year already four basis points from 5.00% and the thirty-year eight from the 2007 peak of 5.44%. A dot showing September as the final move, delivered alongside falling crude from an Oman deal, compresses the ten-year. August retail sales at 8:30 a.m. — consensus 0.2% against 0.5% in July — land in the same session, two hours before equities open: a weak print adds the growth side of the trade-off to the same day as the decision.
trade_setups.entry: 5.00% on the ten-year and 5.44% on the thirty-year are the levels above; 4.90% on a post-decision ten-year rally is the level that would say the market reads the hike as a cycle end rather than a pause.
trade_setups.invalidation: A hold rather than a hike — priced at roughly 15% — would move the market in a direction different from anything in the current consensus, and would likely be accompanied by a press conference statement explaining why the committee waited despite 85% market pricing.

trade_setups.asset: August retail sales — Wednesday September 16, 8:30 a.m. ET
trade_setups.thesis: Retail sales for August print two hours before equities open and ninety minutes before the FOMC statement, creating a live read on the growth side of the trade-off. Consensus is roughly 0.2% against July's 0.5%. Higher gasoline prices may flatter the headline while real spending falls. A weak print puts slowing consumer spending alongside a hike into an oil shock — the growth-versus-inflation tension visible in one morning. A strong print at or above 0.5% says consumption is outrunning the energy shock and removes the dovish framing from the session.
trade_setups.entry: 0.2% is consensus; the relevant threshold is whether the print lands above or below July's 0.5%, since anything below that signals the energy tax is reaching spending. Core retail excluding autos, gas, and food strips the gasoline price effect and is the version to watch if the headline surprises in either direction.
trade_setups.invalidation: An in-line 0.2% print with normal revisions to July leaves the session entirely in the dot plot's hands; neither side of the growth-versus-inflation trade-off is confirmed.
